sections.h2: Three offices behind one tax bill
sections.html:
Three elected offices split the work. One values property and rules on exemptions, one mails and collects the bill, and one records deeds and takes the documentary stamp tax.

The Property Appraiser prepares the real estate and tangible personal property rolls, which fix ownership, mailing address, legal description and value. Your tax is the taxable value after exemptions, multiplied by the millage rate each taxing authority sets. If no bill shows up in November, call the Tax Collector at (352) 374-5236.

  • Value, ownership and exemptions: the Alachua County Property Appraiser (acpafl.org), which also offers a free Title Alert for ownership changes.
  • Bills, payment plans and deferral: the Alachua County Tax Collector.
  • Recorded deeds and doc stamps: the circuit court clerk, who also conducts foreclosure and tax deed sales.

sections.h2: Due dates and early payment discounts
sections.html:
Bills typically arrive near the first of November. The gross amount is payable through the end of March, and delinquency starts April 1. The earlier you pay, the bigger the reduction.

Early payment schedule, by postmark
Postmark monthReduction in the bill
NovemberFour percent off
DecemberThree percent off
JanuaryTwo percent off
FebruaryOne percent off
MarchFull amount, no reduction

Discounts are decided by postmark. After delinquency, April 1 adds a minimum 3 percent charge and May adds an advertising charge, with the total tied to the date the payment is received.

The county's 2026 TRIM explainer shows a 2025 countywide millage of 7.6000 mills and a proposed 2026 rollback rate of 7.2107 mills, which would be the tenth straight year of a lower countywide rate. Treat the 2026 number as proposed until the final rate shows up on your bill or on the Tax Collector's site.

The county is only one line on a TRIM notice. A home inside a city adds that city's levy, and in Gainesville some charges that used to ride on monthly utility bills now appear on the notice. Owners in unincorporated areas may also see a Law Enforcement Municipal Services Taxing Unit line, listed at a proposed 3.5678 mills. Non-ad valorem items such as county fire, solid waste and stormwater are charged by assessment instead of millage.

File with the county appraiser by March 1. To qualify, the house has to be where you lived permanently as of the January 1 before.

The homestead exemption is worth up to $50,000 in taxable value. School taxes only see the first $25,000. The second $25,000 lowers the non-school levies, and only on value above $50,000.

Once you hold homestead, Save Our Homes limits how fast assessed value can rise: 3 percent a year or the CPI change, whichever is smaller. The state chart shows 2.7 percent for 2026. That protection ends with a sale or foreclosure, when value resets to just value the next January. Spousal transfers are among the exceptions.

If you are buying another Florida home, portability can carry the accumulated savings to it, provided the new homestead is set up within three years of giving up the old one. Disabled ex-servicemembers, deployed servicemembers and seniors may have additional relief, and a city or county ordinance sets the senior exemption.

Homestead stops when you rent the house out. Moved already? Ask the Property Appraiser where your status stands before you list.

Two options exist for spreading a bill out or postponing it, each with separate rules: a quarterly installment plan and a homestead tax deferral, both run through the Tax Collector.

The installment plan needs prior year taxes above $100, with applications closing April 30. Discounts are 6 percent on the June 30 payment, 4.5 percent on September 30, 3 percent on December 31, and nothing on March 31.

Deferral is open to a homestead property whose primary mortgage stays within 70 percent of assessed value, with the form due at the end of March. Interest on the deferred amount accrues at up to 7 percent a year. The balance becomes payable all at once if eligibility, use or ownership changes, so selling the house means paying it off at closing.

sections.h2: Landlords and tangible personal property tax
sections.html:
Owning a rental means two taxes: the real estate bill, and tangible personal property tax on whatever furniture, fixtures and equipment are inside.

Tangible property is valued as of January 1. File a return by April 1 and you earn an exemption of up to $25,000. File late, or not at all, and you owe penalties and lose it. Unpaid tangible tax goes delinquent on April 1 with a $10 fee and interest at 1.5 percent a month, and May 1 adds a 20 percent collection fee.

That lien stays attached to the property through a sale, so buyer and seller prorate it at closing. A vacant residential rental may qualify for assessment discounts, and the county's waste collection office, 352-338-3233, can explain.

sections.h2: What happens when taxes go unpaid
sections.html:
After advertising the delinquent parcels, the Tax Collector holds an online certificate sale on lienhub.com by early June. The auction begins at an 18 percent interest rate, and bidders go lower.

Whoever wins pays your tax and earns interest, and the certificate sits first in line against the property. Two or more years after delinquency, its holder can apply for a tax deed, and a parcel nobody redeems is auctioned publicly. You clear a certificate by paying the Tax Collector the tax, interest, costs and charges.

For two years after April 1 of the issue year, Florida law bars the holder from asking the owner for money. If the house carries a certificate, the payoff can usually come out of sale proceeds, and the Tax Collector's office will quote the figure.

The county had 290,028 residents in July 2025. Owners live in 54.1 percent of homes, which signals a big renter base, and the median home value is $288,800. College-town turnover makes title work worth starting early, so order a tax and lien search from your title company the moment a contract is signed.

Whoever is on the roll receives the bill, and the two sides divide the year at closing. A documentary stamp tax of 70 cents per $100 of consideration, outside Miami-Dade, is paid to the clerk as the deed is recorded. All parties on the deed share liability for it, regardless of what the contract says. With a mortgage that escrows taxes, the lender receives the bill and has to pay inside the 4 percent window.

A short routine keeps tax surprises off the settlement statement.

  1. Open your parcel record at the Property Appraiser and check the owner name, mailing address and any exemptions.
  2. Call the Tax Collector and ask whether this year is paid, what is owed, and whether a certificate or installment plan exists.
  3. With a deferral on the property, get the payoff in advance, since the full balance is due on sale.
  4. Give the figures to your title company for the closing statement.

Selling a rental? Add the tangible personal property return to the list. That lien stays with the property after closing.

faqs.q: When does Alachua County mail property tax bills?
faqs.a: Around the start of November. If yours does not arrive, call the Tax Collector at (352) 374-5236.

faqs.q: How long can I wait before Alachua County taxes go delinquent?
faqs.a: Pay by the end of March. After that, a 3 percent minimum charge applies from April 1.

faqs.q: Is the 2026 Alachua County millage final?
faqs.a: The county's explainer shows 7.2107 mills as the proposed 2026 rollback rate, against 7.6000 in 2025. Confirm the final rate with the Tax Collector or on your bill.

faqs.q: Does selling my Alachua County home end my homestead?
faqs.a: A sale counts as a change of ownership, so assessed value returns to just value the next January. The new owner files a fresh homestead application.

faqs.q: Can an Alachua County owner with unpaid tax still sell?
faqs.a: Yes. The title company can pay delinquent tax and any certificate out of the buyer's funds. Ask the Tax Collector for the payoff amount before the closing date.
